newsitem.title: CHILE: RTRS - Threlkeld does not rule out hidden copper stocks.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Threlkeld does not rule out hidden copper stocks.

text.p: Reports which have shaken world copper markets this week that more than 500,000 tonnes of copper lurk hidden in Rotterdam warehouses may be true, said copper trader David Threlkeld.

"Everything is possible and we should not discount anything," Threlkeld --best-known as the man who reported disgraced Japanese trader Yasuo Hamanaka to the LME in the early 1990s-- told reporters at a copper conference in Santiago.

Although rumours that some half a million tonnes of copper lie stacked secretly in Dutch warehouses have largely been dismissed by brokers, studies suggest some copper stocks have vanished from London Metal Exchange (LME), he said.
Market intelligence reports showed 300,000 tonnes of copper disappeared from the LME in 1993, with a similar amount disappearing the following year, he said.
"This would suggest stocks have been underreported by 600,000 tonnes, with consumption overstated during those two years," said Thelkeld.

Copper markets will also continue to be haunted by the secrecy surrounding Hamanaka's deals, suffering great volatility, he said. "Just because Hamanaka has been accused of fraud, does not mean this crisis is over."
He added, "His legacy is still there. The market will go through tremendous turmoil before it finds equilibrium."
Hamanaka was sacked earlier this year and recently charged with fraud in connection with failed trades which cost Sumitomo $2.6 billion in a scandal which rocked world copper markets.
"We know copper was shipped out by Hamanaka and one can no longer presume it was sold physically. Everything the guy did has to be considered suspect," Threlkeld said.
Some physical copper deals signed by Hamanaka with other dealers are still in force, he said.
Threlkeld, who operates his own trading business, called on LME authorities to tighten their controls on futures trading to prevent a similar crisis hitting the market again.
"The LME needs to take meaningful steps to avoid another fiasco," he said.
Threlkeld first alerted authorities to the now notorious Japanese broker when he told the LME that Hamanaka had asked him to fake documents related to copper contracts.
